'When people say things like my ex' implies a breakup/relationship-themed trauma context that is not reflected anywhere in the memory or appraisal items. 'Being naked' likewise suggests a sexual/interpersonal vulnerability cue, but the rest of the profile centers on shame, moral injury, and reliving tied to war-zone experiences rather than sexual trauma. The time-of-day trigger is coherent, but these two triggers pull toward a different trauma narrative and are not supported by the other selected items or formulation-linked nodes.

vignette:
Minh is a 41-year-old contemporary dancer who spent two years as a relief worker in a conflict zone before returning to his wife and his career in a major city. The event that changed everything happened at sunset, during a distribution of medical supplies near the front line. A mortar round struck a nearby fuel depot, and the explosion sent a wall of fire and black smoke rolling over the compound. Minh was knocked flat; the air turned thick with the smell of burnt fuel and something else-medical alcohol from a shattered supply crate that had ignited. He remembers scrabbling to his feet, seeing a colleague pinned under a collapsed wall, and then he ran. He ran away from the fire, away from the screams, and hid behind a concrete barrier until the attack was over. He did not go back until the smoke cleared and it was too late. The colleague died. Minh has never stopped believing that his body made a choice that his mind could not endorse-that he acted in ways that go against who he is, that his instincts as a dancer, trained to move with grace and purpose, failed the one moment they were needed for something real.

Back home, Minh tried to return to the studio as if nothing had happened. But the memory of that sunset, of the alcohol and burnt smells, began ambushing him without warning. He would be stretching before rehearsal when the scent of a nearby bar drifting through a window would snap him back-not just remembering, but reliving: the heat on his skin, the metallic taste in his mouth, the shame that he had not been the person he thought he was. The same time of day became a trap. Every evening, as the light slanted and the sun began to drop, his pulse would spike and his chest would tighten. He started scheduling all his rehearsals for the morning, telling the artistic director he preferred the light. Within months, he had stopped accepting evening performances entirely. His career, which had been building steadily, began to narrow. His wife noticed he no longer wanted to meet friends after work at the bar down the block; he made excuses about his diet, about needing early sleep, but what he could not say was that the smell of alcohol-any alcohol, even a single beer-filled him with a dread that felt like a physical blow. At home, he would leave the room if she burned toast, and he insisted she cook with the exhaust fan on high. She began to feel she was living with a stranger who could be unmoored by a scent in the air.

Minh's shame has only deepened. He sees his avoidance as proof that he is a lousy coper, that his reactions since the event reveal a fundamental weakness. He used to trust his body implicitly-it was his instrument, his source of pride. Now he cannot rely on himself to simply stay in a room where someone is drinking wine, or to walk through a parking lot at dusk. His wife has tried to be patient, but she has started to ask why he won't talk about what happened, and he has no answer that does not feel like more failure. What finally brought Minh to seek help was a recurring moment in rehearsal: the director asked him to perform a solo at a sunset-themed show, and Minh could not even bring himself to say no. He walked out of the studio, shaking, and sat in his car for an hour, gripping the steering wheel. He is terrified that the shame will never lift, that he is stuck with a version of himself he despises. But he is also, beneath everything, hoping that somewhere in the wreckage of his memory there is a way to stop the reliving-to remember the event without feeling, even for a second, that it is still happening now.
